idea: Eratosthenes' measurement of the Earth drawn as a clean geometry diagram in code: sun rays, a well at Syene, an obelisk shadow at Alexandria, a 7.2 degree angle at the centre. Caption: 'Two sticks, one distance, the whole planet.' For people who love a big answer from a tiny measurement.

The longitude problem as a diagram: a globe divided into 24 hour-wedges with a tiny pocket watch at the centre and the line 'One hour of error = 15 degrees = 1,000 miles of wrong.' The shirt for anyone who knows time is the real map.

A compass rose built in code as a precise 32-point wind rose, with each point labelled in old sailor's names (Tramontana, Levante, Ostro, Ponente). Caption: 'Thirty-two ways to be lost, named.' A beautiful object with a wry point of view.

A triangulation diagram in the style of 18th-century survey plates: a baseline, then a web of triangles reaching across a blank page, angles marked. Caption: 'One measured line. Everything else is arithmetic.' For people who admire how maps are made from almost nothing.

Mercator distortion as a code-drawn chart: a column of identical circles (Tissot indicatrices) growing absurdly large toward the poles. Caption: 'Same size. Different latitude.' A smart, quiet argument about whose world we are looking at.

A code-drawn plan of a coastline-paradox diagram: the same island outlined at 200 km, 50 km and 10 km rulers, each longer than the last. Caption: 'How long is the coast? Depends who is asking.' For fractal-minded geography nerds.

A dead-reckoning plot: a ship's track as a series of heading-and-distance vectors, with a growing error ellipse at the end and a question mark in its centre. Caption: 'Here, approximately.' Humble, funny and nautical.

The sextant explained: a public-domain engraving of a sextant with the geometry of double reflection overlaid in lines, labelled 'Sun. Horizon. You.' For those who love knowing exactly where they stand.

A map drawn entirely of place names, no coastline: the words 'Terra Incognita' in the middle, ringed by the real names explorers gave to capes of disappointment (Cape Farewell, Point Hope, Mount Misery, Cape Fear) in positions that suggest a shore. Caption: 'Named by someone having a day.' Typographic, wry, and buildable as type.

A hand-drawn-in-code contour map of an imaginary hill, with the elevation labelled in a spiral so the contour lines read as a fingerprint. Caption: 'Every hill has a signature.' For hikers who like topology more than summits.

A diagram of Polynesian wayfinding from open archive sources: a star compass with the houses of rising and setting stars, wave swell arrows and a bird flight line. Caption: 'No instruments. Everything else.' A respectful celebration of navigation by knowing.

A great-circle versus rhumb-line diagram on an old engraved globe: the curved shortest path against the straight compass line, labelled 'Straight is not the shortest.' A tidy paradox for people who like being right on the details.

The Harrison H4 chronometer cutaway from a public-domain plate, with a callout arrow reading 'This is what 20,000 pounds looked like.' For horology and exploration nerds who like the object that solved the problem.
A magnetic declination chart in the style of Halley's 1701 isogonic map, redrawn as clean code lines, captioned 'North moves.' A short, unsettling fact for compass owners.

A Voronoi diagram built in code from the world's actual capital cities, no coastlines, each cell a territory of nearest-capital. Caption: 'Your nearest capital.' Abstract, beautiful, and secretly a map.

The Eratosthenes-style 'Ptolemy's grid' projection diagram: a conic projection's fan of meridians with parallels, labelled in Latin, and one small note: 'Flattening a sphere: still unsolved.' A scholarly joke about the impossible task of mapmaking.

A tide-and-current chart of a harbour approach in the style of 19th-century Admiralty plates, with soundings in tiny numbers and one phrase: 'Depths in fathoms. Mistakes in feet.' For sailors and lovers of quiet number-covered charts.

A diagram of a stadia-rod survey in the field: a theodolite, a rod, sightlines, and the labels 'Know your height. Know your distance.' Archive survey plate style. For anyone who likes careful, slow measuring.

A map projection family drawn in code: eight small globes flattened eight ways, labelled with surnames (Mercator, Mollweide, Robinson, Peters, Goode, Winkel, Gall, Lambert). Caption: 'Eight lies about the same place.' For anyone who loves a fair-minded argument.

An overland expedition route diagram: a dotted line across empty space with day counts, camps numbered, and the final marker reading 'Turned back here. Wise.' Archive map style. A rare tribute to knowing when to stop.
